steps: Assemble before placing

The flue collar ships on top; for a rear exit, remove its two M6 bolts (10 mm wrench), turn it to the rear and refit. Take out the loose front ash lip and fit any accessories before the stove goes into its final position.

• Hold the M6 flange nuts inside the collar so they don't fall into the stove; re-use the same bolts and M6 fender washers.
  • The front ash lip and the combustor monitor ship inside the stove. The monitor is installed per section 5.6 (last step).
  • Install accessories with their own instructions: Rear Heatshield 158374 (the only heat shield allowed); Blower Kit 156431 (thermostatic, 120 cfm, must be installed with Rear Heat Shield 158374, not included); Outside Air Kit 154335 (3 inch adapter; also needs metallic flex pipe, a rain/weather resistant cap and a rodent screen no larger than 1/4" mesh).
Chimney connector

6" single-wall pipe, min. 24 gauge black steel, crimped ends toward the stove, three sheet metal screws per joint and two self-drilling screws at the collar. Max 36" horizontal run rising 1/4" per foot, no more than two 90° elbows.

Recommended total stove pipe length: no more than 10 feet. No aluminum or galvanized pipe. Never through an attic or roof space, closet or other concealed space, floor or ceiling; every section accessible for cleaning. Don't use connector pipe as a chimney or connect to a flue serving another appliance.
Chimney

Code-approved masonry chimney with flue liner, or a UL 103 Type HT (2100°F) prefab chimney; an existing chimney must pass a UL 1482 Level II inspection. Flue area: not less than the flue collar, not more than three times it.

• Interior masonry: up to three times the collar area; with one or more walls exposed outside below the roofline, up to two times. Reline larger flues with a listed or code-approved liner.
  • Fireclay liner min. 5/8" thick in refractory mortar, at least 1/4" air space to the chimney wall; nominal 8" X 8", no larger than 8" X 12"; round liners 6" to 8" inside diameter.
  • Brick or block wall min. 4" nominal; rubble stone at least 12". Airtight clean-out door at the base. No other appliance on the flue.
  • Height: minimum 15 feet (4.57 m); 3 feet above the roof penetration and 2 feet above anything within 10 feet (p. 8). Prefab: UL 103 HT / ULC S629, clearance per the pipe maker.
  • Not for installation in a factory-built fireplace.

Canada only (p. 6): a continuous 6" liner to the top of the chimney, to CAN/ULC-S635 Class 3 or CAN/ULC-S640. That paragraph refers to a "fireplace insert".
Wall pass-through

Consult local officials first. U.S. NFPA 211 common method: clear combustibles 12" around the connector (31" x 31" with a 6" liner), fill with 12" of solid brick around a fireclay liner, at least 18" from the ceiling.

U.S. (NFPA 211 common method)

  • Fireclay liner ASTM C35 or equivalent, min. 5/8" wall; solid brick min. 3 1/4" thick (4" nominal).
  • Cut studs, add headers and a sill frame to carry the brick. Refractory mortar at the chimney junction; the pass-through liner must not go past the inner surface of the chimney liner (tiles shatter easily).

Canada (CAN/CSA-B365 common method)

  • Clear combustibles at least 18" around the connector; a 6" round liner needs a 43" x 43" opening; at least 18" from combustible ceiling materials.
  • Leave the cleared space empty. Sheet metal covers on both sides go on noncombustible spacers at least 1" off the wall; a single panel may be flush.
Connect to the chimney

Masonry thimble lined and cemented; the connector slides in to the flue liner's inner surface without protruding and is sealed with refractory cement. Hearthmount: seal the masonry flue from room air. Prefab: maker's adaptor, three sheet metal screws.

• A slip-connector may be used at the thimble for adjustment and cleaning access.
  • Hearthmount (NFPA 211 12.4.5.1): replace the damper with a fixed steel plate the connector passes through to the first flue tile, or a non-combustible plate at the fireplace opening, sealed with high-temperature sealant; or a full listed liner to a sealed chimney cap. Jøtul recommends a block-off plate in the damper area.
  • Rear exit flue collar height: 28 1/4" (718 mm) on standard legs, 26" (660 mm) with short legs. Oversized liner: install a code-approved relining system.
  • Hearthmounts must also meet the mantel and trim clearances (p. 14) and floor protection (p. 11). Fig. 3.2 shows the construction, including a maximum-depth dimension; check the drawing.
Floor protection + bottom heat shield

Bolt the supplied bottom heat shield to the stove bottom (required). Use a listed UL 1618 floor protector unless on concrete over earth: U.S. 16" front and 8" each side (33"W X 40"D); Canada 18" front, 8" sides and back (41"W X 48"D).

1. Bend the flat heat shield on its perforations, painted side down.
  2. Remove the two bolts from the bottom of the ash compartment (10 mm wrench).
  3. Attach the shield to the stove bottom with those bolts, oriented as in Fig. 4.3 (p. 13).

Continuous non-combustible material; sections mortared or sealed; carpet removed. Rear vent: extend under the pipe at least 2" (50mm) beyond each side. Alcoves: minimum R-value of 1.6. Alternate materials: compare total R-value with the specified protector (method on pp. 11-12).
Clearances & shields

Set side, rear and corner clearances from the p. 14 table (no shield, single-wall pipe: 14" / 16" / 13" unprotected). Reduce them only with Rear Heatshield 158374, listed connector shields or listed double-wall pipe.

Pipe shields start 1" above the lowest exposed point of the connector and extend at least 25" above the stove top. Wall-mounted protection per NFPA 211. Combustibles include sheet rock, wallpaper, wood and fabrics, even behind non-combustible facing; fire-resistant materials and fire-rated sheet rock count as combustible. Keep airflow in the clearance space open.
Alcove (if used)

Listed double-wall pipe; NFPA 211 protection on both side walls and the rear wall, spaced 1" off the floor and 1" off the wall, 48" high. Bottom heat shield plus a UL/ULC listed Type II Thermal Floor Protector or material of min. R-value 1.6.

Minimum ceiling height above the stove top: 41" (1041 mm) unprotected, 15" (380mm) with a protected ceiling. Clearances are measured from the stove plates to the combustible wall. The alcove clearance and size limits are shown only in Figs. 4.4-4.5 on p. 13; read them from the drawings.
Mobile home (if used)

Secure the stove with Floor Mounting Kit #750304 and connect outside air with Outside Air Kit #154335 (duct no higher than the stove's air inlet). UL 103 chimney attached directly, at least 3 ft above the roof, removable at or below 13.5 ft for transport, with a spark arrester.

• Maintain the structural integrity of floor, walls and ceiling/roof.
  • Termination at least 2 ft (0.6m) above any part of the home within 10 ft (3m).
  • Spark arrester: net free area at least four times the chimney outlet, height at least one-half the flue diameter; openings stop a 1/2" (12.7 mm) sphere and pass a 3/8" (9.6 mm) sphere.
  • Chimney exiting other than through the roof at 7 ft (2.1 m) or less above ground: guard it up to 7 ft; openings must not admit a 3/4 in. rod, or let a 1/2 inch rod inserted 4 inches touch the chimney.
  • Do not install the stove in a bedroom or sleeping area.
Combustor monitor + first fires

Remove the lower set screw on the right side panel (3mm hex key; leave the upper one), reorient the probe magnet and push the monitor fully into the hole. Before any hot fire, the owner runs the three break-in fires.

The upper set screw holds the top plate to the sides. Push the magnet up to the washer (Figs. 5.6-5.8, p. 20). Monitor PN 226609.

Chimney draft should be in the .05 - 1.0 w.c. range (as printed, p. 20). Break-in: about 1 hour at 200°F, 1 hour at up to 400°F, then 500°F, cooling to room temperature between fires (pp. 20-21).

items: Back puffing: smoke leaks into the room at stove or connector joints

Exhaust fan or clothes dryer: low pressure, flow reversal (Outside Air Kit #154335 may help)

Correct with a butterfly damper; consult the dealer

items: Loss of heating efficiency, more creosote and emissions
Test: medium to high fire for two or three hours over 500°F, then air at medium to medium low

Junk mail or heavy newsprint starts speed fly ash buildup

fire.title: Starting a fire
fire.html:
Don't raise the fire up in any way, and never use gasoline, kerosene, lighter fluid or similar liquids to start or freshen up a fire. If the stove is new, do the three break-in fires first.

Top-down method (less start-up smoke)

  1. Move the air lever fully to the right (open). Lay two short 1/4-split logs on the firebox floor, at right angles to the back wall, about 6 inches apart.
  2. Lay kindling across them, then one or two smaller logs on top.
  3. Tuck newspaper between the two bottom logs, under the kindling. Light it and close the door.
  4. Add kindling and small logs as needed. Keep the air fully open until the fire is well established.

Traditional method

With the lever fully right, crumple several sheets of newspaper directly on the grate. Add small dry kindling (about 1" thick) and two or three small logs (about 3" to 5"). Light it, close the door, and build up slowly with larger logs. Then set the air for the heat and burn time you want (see Set the air control).

Build the fire directly on the stove's own bottom grate (p. 21); the grate is a standard part of the stove. The safety notices say not to use a grate or elevate the fire, and to build it directly on the hearth (p. 4): that means don't add a separate grate or anything else that raises the fire.

Keep the ash pan door closed whenever the stove is burning.

breakin.title: Breaking in a new stove
breakin.html:
Cast iron expands and contracts as it heats and cools, so a new stove needs a gradual warm-up: three small-to-medium fires. Watch a stove-top thermometer.

  1. Open the air fully. Light a small fire of newspaper and kindling. Let the stove top reach only 200°F (93°C), hold it there for about 1 hour, then let the stove cool to room temperature.
  2. Light a second fire and let the stove reach no more than 400°F (204°C) for 1 hour. Let it cool to room temperature.
  3. Light a third fire and gradually bring the stove up to 500°F (260°C) and hold it there. Let it cool to room temperature. Break-in is done.
If one of the first two fires goes past 400°F, move the air lever all the way left. The temperature may keep climbing until the wood burns down a bit; that's normal. Never pull burning logs out to cool the stove.

Smoke and smell at first

A new painted stove gives off some odor and smoke during its first fires while the high-temperature paint and materials cure. Open a window or door for extra fresh air.

air.title: Setting the air control
air.html:
The primary air lever is at the front center, just below the door. Far left is fully closed; far right is fully open. More air makes a hotter, faster fire. Moving the lever left gives a longer, lower burn. Start or revive a fire with the lever fully right.

Secondary air, which feeds the catalytic combustor, is set automatically. There's nothing for you to adjust.

Settings guide

LowFully to the left
Medium low3/16" to the right
Medium high3/8" to the right
HighFully to the right

With the optional blower: minimum speed for low and medium low, medium for medium high, high for high.

Note: the manual gives different points for turning the air down: p. 19 says fully open for the first five minutes, and mid-range once the stove top reaches 400°F - 600°F; p. 20 says open until the combustor monitor reads 500°F, then hold that for 15-20 minutes; p. 21 says adjust once the stove top reads 500° to 600°.

Keep a stove-top thermometer in either rear corner. Short spells at 700-800 won't harm the stove; long periods in that range can. The low setting is fixed at the factory, and altering it is against federal regulations.

reload.title: Reloading the stove
reload.html:
Reload while there's still a bed of hot embers. Always wear gloves when tending the stove.

  1. Push the air lever fully to the right (open).
  2. Open the door slightly at first, then fully. This lets the airflow settle so less smoke spills out.
  3. Use a stove tool or poker to spread the hot embers evenly, away from the air inlets at the front center of the firebox floor.
  4. Load the wood, usually smaller logs first. Keep logs off the glass.
  5. Close the door and latch it tightly.
  6. Wait 5 – 10 minutes, then set the air for the heat you want. With an ember bed at least 2" thick, you may be able to set it right away.
Don't overload. Keep the wood below the holes in the air baffle. A traditional three-log load is safest and looks best.

Empty the ash pan before you reload, while the fire is low, and keep the ash door shut while the stove burns.

catalyst.title: The catalytic combustor
catalyst.html:
The catalytic combustor sits at the top of the firebox and burns smoke that would otherwise go up the chimney. Running the stove with it deactivated or removed is against federal regulations.

Read the monitor

The combustor monitor on the right side shows the catalyst's temperature. It does its work between 500°F and 1200°F, and the most efficient range is 500°F to 800°. Readings over 1,400°F aren't unusual. Do not over-fire the stove: keep the combustor at or below 1600°F. Above 1750°F, even briefly, it can be damaged.

Note: p. 20 prints the most efficient range as 500°F and 800°, with a Celsius range of 260°C - 371°C. The two upper figures don't match.

Signs it's working

  • Above 500°F, look up through the glass: jets of flame come from the baffle ports and the catalyst glows vividly red.
  • Little or no smoke leaves the chimney.

Keep it clean

  • Look at it at least three times each heating season: open the door and look up at the catalyst with a flashlight.
  • Sweep loose fly ash off the cells with a soft brush. A shop vacuum works if you're careful; the cells are fragile.
  • Starting fires with junk mail or lots of newspaper clogs it faster.

A performance check is on p. 26.

wood.title: What wood to burn
wood.html:
This stove is made to burn natural wood only. Air-dried, seasoned hardwood burns more efficiently and cleaner than softwood or green wood.

  • Air-dry wood for 6 to 14 months. Wood seasoned more than 2 years burns too quickly.
  • Seasoned logs have many cracks in the ends and feel lighter than fresh ones.
  • Check with a moisture meter that has probes. Aim for 12 - 20% on the gauge. Wetter wood wastes heat and leaves creosote in the chimney.
  • Logs can be up to 20" long. Keep them off the glass so air can move.
  • Store wood somewhere dry, outside the stove's clearance area.

Never burn

Coal, garbage, synthetic fuel or logs, rubber, plastics, waste petroleum or asphalt products, paints, thinners or solvents, asbestos, construction or demolition debris, railroad ties or pressure-treated wood, manure or animal remains, yard waste, salt-water driftwood, unseasoned wood, colored paper, junk mail, cardboard, plywood or particle board. Fire starters made from paper, cardboard, sawdust or wax are fine for lighting.

These can give off toxic fumes, including carbon monoxide, and can permanently ruin the catalytic combustor, which voids its warranty.

clean.title: Ashes, glass and door seals
clean.html:
Empty the ash pan

The ash pan is behind a door under the front ash lip, so you don't need to open the front door. Turn the handle counterclockwise to open and clockwise to latch. Empty it before reloading, when the fire is low or out. Wear stove gloves, and close the ash door before you carry the ashes away.

Put ashes in a metal container with a tight lid. Set it on a noncombustible floor or on the ground, well away from anything that can burn, until the cinders are completely cool. Only use a vacuum made for ashes. Leave a one inch bed of ashes on the firebox floor.

Clean the glass

Use only an ammonia-free, non-abrasive stove glass cleaner, and only when the glass is at room temperature. Deposits left on too long can etch and cloud it.

Test the door seals

Close and latch the door on a dollar bill, then slowly pull. You should feel resistance; if it slides out easily, the seal is too loose. Check several spots, and the ash pan door too. A loose front door can be tightened by removing a latch shim (p. 24).

chimney.title: Chimney and creosote
chimney.html:
Slow fires and green wood make creosote, a tar that collects in the chimney. It's highly flammable, and it's what fuels chimney fires.

Inspect and sweep

  • Inspect the chimney and connector pipe at the start of each heating season, then every other month during it.
  • Clean them whenever creosote and fly ash build up more than 1/4 inch anywhere. Your Jøtul dealer sells chimney brushes and can refer you to a professional chimney sweep.
  • When the stove is run well, brushing the flue brings down mostly fly ash, with little creosote.

If you suspect a chimney fire

You may hear a roaring noise and crackling as flakes of burning creosote break loose.

  1. Close the air control right away (lever fully left) and make sure the stove door is closed.
  2. Call the fire department and get everyone out of the house.
  3. Don't try to put out the fire in the stove. When the noise dies down, don't open the door to check; the fire could rekindle.
  4. Don't use the stove again until the chimney and connector have been cleaned and inspected.

safety.title: Safety and over-firing
safety.html:
• The stove gets extremely hot. Keep children, clothing and furniture away, and use a child guard screen for small children.
  • Burn only with the front door fully closed. A door left partly open can cause over-firing and let flame and smoke out.
  • Keep the ash pan door closed while the stove burns. Open it only long enough to empty the pan.
  • Don't run the stove with broken glass, and don't strike the glass or slam the door.
  • Put smoke and carbon monoxide (CO) detectors in the living area and bedrooms. Test them regularly and fit fresh batteries twice a year. In the stove's room, mount one as far from the stove as you can.
  • Exhaust fans and clothes dryers can lower the air pressure in the room and make air flow backward through the stove and chimney.

Signs of over-firing

Do not over-fire the stove. If any part of the stove or chimney connector glows, other than the combustor, you're over-firing. That can cause a house fire or serious damage, and the warranty won't cover it. Warped plates, rust-colored cast iron, paint turned dusty white, or bubbling, cracked enamel are also signs.

Note: the operating warnings leave the combustor out of the glow rule (pp. 4, 17), and it glows vividly red when working (p. 20); the warranty says over-firing occurs when any part of the stove glows red (p. 30).

warranty.title: Warranty at a glance
warranty.html:
Jøtul's warranty (effective January 1, 2019) covers the original retail purchaser from the date of purchase and can't be transferred.

Baffle & air manifold partsLimited lifetime, parts only
Cast iron & steel parts5 years
Enamel finish (peeling, fading)2 years
Blowers, thermostatic switches, combustion monitor1 year
High Flow catalytic combustor10 years
Note: part A gives baffle and air-manifold components a limited lifetime warranty, but exclusion 1 lists baffles and air manifolds among wear parts that aren't covered (p. 30).

Not covered

  • Wear parts: paint, gaskets, burn plates, firebricks, fire grates, and glass (covered only for thermal breakage).
  • Damage from over-firing, misuse or improper operation, such as burning with the ash door open.
  • Installation or service by someone other than an authorized installer or service agency, or not following the manual and local codes.

Keep your dated receipt. Jøtul must hear about a possible defect within 60 days of finding it; claims go through your nearest authorized Jøtul dealer. A second combustor failure within the 10 years is covered at 50% off current retail.

conflicts.issue: Minimum chimney height is given as 15 feet (4.57 m), while the same section says chimneys shorter than 14 feet may not provide adequate draft.

When to turn the primary air down: lever at Full Open for the first five minutes (p. 19 table note); stove-top 400°F - 600°F before a mid-range setting (p. 19); fully open until the combustor monitor registers 500°F, then 15-20 minutes (p. 20); adjust once the stovetop reads 500° and 600° (p. 21).

Safety notices say 'do not use a grate or elevate the fire; build the fire directly on the hearth' (p. 4); section 5.8 says to burn 'directly on the bottom grate of the stove' and lay newspaper on the grate (p. 21); the parts list includes 'Grate, F 445' 105035 (p. 29).
conflicts.reason: The p. 4 safety notice bars using a grate or elevating the fire; section 5.8 (p. 21) says to burn directly on the bottom grate of the stove and also not to elevate the fire, and that grate is a standard part of this stove (parts list p. 29: 77. Grate, F 445, 105035). Read together: no added grate; build the fire on the stove's own bottom grate. Reworded in the drawer; box removed.

conflicts.issue: Optimum combustor range printed as 500°F and 800° with Celsius 260°C - 371°C; the upper Fahrenheit and Celsius figures don't correspond.
Section A gives baffle and air manifold components a limited lifetime warranty (parts only); exclusion 1 lists baffles and air manifolds among normal-wear parts not covered.

Over-firing is any part of the stove or connector glowing except the combustor (pp. 4, 17), and a working catalyst glows vividly red (p. 20); the warranty says over-firing occurs when any part of the stove glows red (p. 30).
Canadian minimum floor protection width is 41" (1041mm) in the text and Fig. 4.2 (p. 11), but the p. 15 clearance diagrams label the Canadian hearth 42''.
The luxury vinyl flooring note (no LVF within 57" of the stove front) names the F 500 V3, not the F 445.

review.notes: Catalytic wood stove: no gas ignition, no error/LED code table (codes empty). The manual has no troubleshooting chart; fault panels are built from its draft, over-firing and combustor descriptions (pp. 4, 7-8, 17, 19, 26-27, 30). Catalog checked against p. 3/p. 6/p. 16: heat output range, 55,000 BTU max, 1600 sq ft, 9 h, HHV 72%, .49 g/hr, 20" logs, 6" flue, EPA 2020, catalytic, mobile-home approval, blower and outside-air kits all agree. Weight (418 lb) and firebox volume (2.03 cu ft) are not in the manual, so they are omitted, not mismatches. Overall dimensions appear only on the p. 5 drawings (26 1/4", 29", 25" with no axis labels in the text; Fig. 1.3 rear-exit centre-line value unreadable): not transcribed; rear-exit height uses the p. 10 text (28 1/4" / 26"). Not transcribed from figures: p. 15 clearance diagrams (pipe positions, corner values), alcove clearances and size limits (Figs. 4.4-4.5, p. 13), unexplained Fig. 4.1/4.2 labels (6" sides, 50,5" depth, 56" width), and the Fig. 3.2 'Max Depth is 10" measured from the front of the front leg' hearthmount note. Printed oddities kept as printed: chimney draft '.05 - 1.0 w.c.' (p. 20); stove-top '700-800' with no unit (p. 19); 'UL 1482 Level II inspection' (p. 6); mobile-home chimney 'UL 103 Standard for 650°C Factory-built Chimneys' (p. 16). Cross-reference errors: p. 4 sends break-in to 'Sect. 5.6' (it is 5.7); p. 16 sends outside air to 'page 15' (kit is on p. 2); p. 2 TOC pages are wrong for 6.3 and from 6.6 on (actual: chimney system p. 23, gaskets p. 24, combustion maintenance p. 26, combustor replacement pp. 26-27, parts pp. 28-29, warranty pp. 30-32).p. 6 'Canada only' liner paragraph calls the unit a 'fireplace insert'. p. 22 mentions burning 'with the screen in place' but no screen is listed for this stove: omitted. Enamel care (p. 23) left out of owner tiles (parts list shows matte black only). 'Do not install the stove in a bedroom or sleeping area' sits in the mobile-home section (p. 16) and is shown in that step. Combustor warranty: p. 32 says a second failure is 50% off current retail and 'any subsequent replacement' is at current retail; summarised without resolving. No French-only or scrambled text in this manual. Website (website.json, Oct 12): weight 418 lb is not in the manual, so skipped; height/width/depth 29 / 26.25 / 25 match the p. 5 drawing values (not transcribed); log size, emissions, burn time, 1600 sq ft, EPA 2020 and the 33" W x 40" D hearth agree; 'height with optional short legs 26.75 in' is overall height, a different measure from the manual's 26" rear-exit height, so not shown.
